name: Design a Data Deletion and Privacy Platform
intent: Honour "delete my data" and "export my data" requests across 200 services and hundreds of data stores within 30 days: find every copy, erase it from stores that cannot be edited, prove it happened, and never delete what the law says to keep.
codeTitle: a deletion orchestrator with a data map, retries, a legal hold and key shredding
finalIntro: One "delete my account and data" request, from the verified form to the proof.
prompt: Design the platform that handles data subject requests for a company with 40 million active accounts and 200 services. A user can ask to download everything the company holds about them, or to have it all erased. Personal data sits in operational databases, search indexes, caches, a 600 TB data lake of immutable files, an analytics warehouse, event logs, 35 days of backups and a dozen third-party processors. The law gives 30 days to finish. Some data must be kept for tax or because of a lawsuit, and the company must be able to show a regulator that it did what it said without keeping the data it deleted.
functional: Accept an export or deletion request through the app or support, after verifying the person's identity
Keep a data map of every kind of personal data, the stores that hold it, and the way to read or erase it there
Fan a request out to every store as tasks, track each to completion, retry failures and chase the third parties
Soft-delete at once so the account disappears, then hard-delete after a short grace period
Erase from immutable stores such as lake files, event logs and backups without rewriting history
Block deletion of anything under a legal hold or a legal retention duty, and say so to the user
Build an export bundle of the person's data in a readable format
Keep a proof of deletion that shows what was erased where and when, without containing the data
nonFunctional: Every request finishes within 30 days, with an internal target of 14 days and an alarm at day 20
About 270 requests a day on average and several thousand a day after a news story or a breach
Zero personal data left in a store the data map knows about, and a way to find stores it does not know about
A deleted person never comes back, even after a database restore
A request by someone who is not the account owner must never delete or export anything
Held or legally retained data is never erased by accident
The proof of deletion is kept for years and contains no personal data

firstAttempt.text: A support engineer runs a script on request. It deletes the user's row from the main users database, clears the cache key and replies "done". Export is a manual query over the same database. A spreadsheet lists the people who asked, and the date is written down when someone remembers.
limits: The user's data is in dozens of other places the script knows nothing about: search indexes, the warehouse, the lake, logs, backups and vendors
A script that fails halfway leaves no record of which stores were cleaned, and nobody retries the rest
Files in the lake and the backups cannot be edited in place, so the data stays for as long as the files do
Nothing checks legal holds, so a person involved in a lawsuit can be erased by a script run in good faith
Anyone who can send an email can ask for someone else's data, because nobody verifies identity
There is no clock, no alarm at day 20 and no proof for the regulator except a spreadsheet
A restored backup brings the deleted rows back, and nobody notices

steps.title: Verify who is asking, and record the request
steps.problem: A request to delete or export is one of the most dangerous calls in the company. If an attacker can send one in someone else's name, they can destroy an account or walk away with a full copy of a stranger's life.
steps.fix: All requests enter through one intake API. The signed-in user re-authenticates (a fresh password or passkey check, plus a one-time code to the verified email or phone) before a request is accepted. Requests from support or by email use a verification link sent to the address on file, never to the address in the request. The API stores a request record with an id, a type (export, delete or both), the verified subject, the receipt time and a due date 30 days later. It checks that the same person has no request open, so retries do not create copies, and it answers with the request id and the due date. The account is soft-deleted straight away: it is hidden, sign-in is blocked and sessions are revoked, but nothing is erased for a grace period of a few days in which the user can cancel.
steps.tradeoff: A forged or hasty request cannot destroy anything permanent, and the legal clock starts from a record nobody can quietly edit. The cost is friction for the real user and a support queue for people who cannot pass verification. The grace period delays the hard delete by days, which must be counted inside the 30.

steps.title: Keep a data map of where every kind of personal data lives
steps.problem: You cannot delete what you cannot find. With 200 services and about 400 data stores, no one person knows where an email address, a device id or a delivery address ends up, and new copies appear every week.
steps.fix: Build a data map, a registry of data categories and the stores that hold them. Each entry names the store, its owner team, the personal data fields in it, the key that links the data to a person (user id, email, device id), the way to export it, the way to erase it (delete rows, delete documents, shred a key, call a vendor API) and how long it may be kept. Teams declare their stores when they ship, because a schema change or a new table that adds a personal field is blocked by the pipeline until the registry entry exists. A scanner samples stores and the lake for email-shaped and phone-shaped values and opens a ticket when it finds personal data in a place that is not in the map.
steps.tradeoff: Deletion becomes a list of known tasks instead of a hunt. The map is only as complete as the teams are honest, so it needs the pipeline gate, the scanner and an owner for every entry. Keeping it accurate is a permanent cost, and it is the part of the system that auditors will read first.

steps.title: Fan out tasks from an orchestrator and track each one
steps.problem: One request means about 60 tasks across stores run by different teams. Some are down for a deploy, some are slow, and a vendor takes a week. A script that stops at the first error finishes nothing and tells nobody.
steps.fix: An orchestrator reads the data map, works out which stores hold this person (a lookup in an identity graph of the person's ids), and writes one task per store with a state: pending, running, done, failed or blocked. Tasks go on a queue and store connectors carry them out. A connector knows how to read and erase in its store and must be idempotent, because a task will be delivered twice. Failures retry with exponential backoff and a cap, and the orchestrator keeps the state, so a crash resumes where it stopped. A request is complete only when every task is done. Tasks have deadlines: an internal target at day 14, an alarm to the owning team at day 20 and a page at day 25. Exports use the same machinery, with read tasks that stream rows into an encrypted bundle which the user downloads through a link that expires in 7 days.
steps.tradeoff: Every request has an exact status, a retry history and a clock, and slow teams are visible. The orchestrator holds the full list of where a person's data is, so it needs strong access control and its own retention. The task table is bigger than the problem looks: at 270 requests a day and 60 tasks each, about 480,000 tasks are open in any 30-day window.

steps.title: Erase from immutable stores by destroying a per-user key
steps.problem: The data lake holds 600 TB in columnar files that are never edited, and one person's rows are spread across millions of files. Rewriting every file that holds a deleted user would read and write hundreds of terabytes a week. Event logs and derived tables are the same: they are append-only copies, and a model feature table is built from the data.
steps.fix: Encrypt personal fields in the lake and in event logs with a key per person. The key lives in a key store (wrapped by a master key in a key management service), and writers look it up when they write. To erase the person, the connector deletes their key. The ciphertext still sits in the files, but it can no longer be read by anyone, including the company, which is crypto-shredding. A small number of fields that need joins, such as a pseudonymous id, stay in clear and are not personal data on their own. Derived tables are rebuilt from the lake in their normal schedule, and anything that kept raw personal data is a separate map entry with its own task: delete the rows, or drop the person's partition at the next compaction.
steps.tradeoff: Erasure costs one key delete instead of hundreds of terabytes of rewriting, and it is instant. Every write and read pays for a key lookup, so keys are cached, and the key store becomes critical: lose it and the data is gone for everyone, back it up with care but never with keys of people who were deleted. Data that was written without a key still needs a rewrite, done once and in bulk, with the next compaction.

steps.title: Expire backups, replay the deletions on restore, and chase vendors
steps.problem: Backups are full copies that must not be edited, and they hold the data for 35 days. A restore after an outage would bring deleted people back. Third-party processors such as the email service, the support desk and the analytics vendor hold copies that the company does not run.
steps.fix: Backups are not edited. They expire on their normal schedule, and the privacy notice says that data in backups is put beyond use and is gone after 35 days, which the regulators accept as long as it is true. The orchestrator keeps a replay-deletion list of every person erased in the last 35 days, as salted hashes of their ids. A restore job must apply the list to the restored database before it takes traffic, and the restore runbook is not finished until it did. For vendors, a connector calls the vendor's deletion API with the person's identifiers, keeps the vendor's receipt and polls for confirmation. Vendors with no API get a ticket with a due date and a named owner.
steps.tradeoff: Backups stay untouched and trustworthy, and no deleted person returns. Erasure in backups is finished only after 35 days, which is longer than the deadline, so the rule has to be written down and stay true. The list is small, about 9,000 ids in 35 days at 270 a day, but a restore that forgets it is a legal incident. Vendors are the slowest and least reliable tasks, and the company stays responsible for them.

steps.title: Respect legal holds, prove the deletion, and apply retention rules
steps.problem: Not everything may be deleted. A lawsuit, an investigation or a tax rule can require the company to keep some of a person's data, and deleting it by mistake is as serious as keeping it by mistake. A regulator also wants proof that deletion happened, but the proof cannot hold the data it proves was removed.
steps.fix: A legal holds service is checked before every hard-delete task, not only at intake, so a hold placed on day 10 still stops a task due on day 12. A held person's data stays, the request moves to a blocked state, and the user is told that part of the request is on hold, without saying why if the law forbids it. Retention rules from the data map split the request: invoices stay for 7 years for tax and are cut off from every other use, and everything else goes. When a hold is released, the blocked tasks resume with a short deadline. Each completed task writes a signed entry to a proof ledger: request id, a salted hash of the person id, store, method (rows deleted, key shredded, vendor receipt), time and the connector's version. The ledger is append-only and has no personal data in it.
steps.tradeoff: A held request is never erased by accident, and the company can show a regulator a signed history of what was done where. A hash of an id is still personal data in some readings of the law, so the salt is secret and kept apart. The ledger is kept for years while the data is not, which is the only copy of the fact that someone asked. Holds make some requests take much longer than 30 days, and that has to be told to the user.

failures.scenario: A vendor's deletion API is down for six days
failures.impact: One task in every request stays open, the requests cannot be completed and the 30-day clock keeps running for hundreds of people.
failures.answer: The connector retries with backoff and a cap, so a short outage heals itself. The orchestrator marks the task stalled after 24 hours and alerts the vendor's owner. At day 20 the request escalates to a page and a support ticket to the vendor with the due date. Everything else in the request is finished, and the proof ledger shows which task is open. If the vendor cannot comply, the company records that and may stop using the vendor, but a task is never silently marked done.

failures.scenario: A database is restored from backup after an outage
failures.impact: The restored copy is 12 hours old and contains people who were hard-deleted since then. They reappear in the product and in marketing emails.
failures.answer: The restore runbook has a final step that applies the replay-deletion list of the last 35 days to the restored database, by salted hash, before it is put back in service. The step is a gate in the restore tool, not a note in a wiki, and it writes an entry to the proof ledger. A check after each drill counts deleted ids that are present, and it must be zero.

failures.scenario: A team ships a new service that stores email addresses and never registers it
failures.impact: Deletion requests complete on the map, but the person's email stays in a store the platform has never heard of. The company is non-compliant while the dashboard says "done".
failures.answer: The release pipeline blocks a service that creates storage or adds a personal field without a data map entry, so this should not ship at all. The scanner is the second line: it samples stores and the lake for personal values and opens a ticket for any hit that is not in the map. When a gap is found, a new entry is added and a back-fill task runs over everyone who has been deleted since the store appeared.

failures.scenario: A legal hold is placed on day 10 for a person whose request is half done
failures.impact: Some data has been erased already and some tasks are queued for day 12. Erasing the rest would destroy evidence under a court order.
failures.answer: The hold check runs just before each hard-delete task executes, not only when the task is created, so queued tasks turn into blocked at once. Tasks that finished cannot be undone, which is why soft delete and the grace period come first and why legal tells the platform early. The record shows exactly which stores were erased before the hold. After the hold is released the remaining tasks run with a short deadline.

failures.scenario: An attacker takes over an account and asks for deletion and an export
failures.impact: The real owner loses the account, and the attacker walks away with a bundle of the owner's personal data.
failures.answer: Intake requires a fresh authentication and a code to the verified contact on file, and a request made within days of a password or email change is held for review. The account is soft-deleted first, so the owner has a window to cancel from the email that was sent to the old address. Export links are single-use, expire in 7 days and are encrypted with a key the requester proves they hold. Every request is rate limited and appears in the user's security notifications.

alternatives.title: Erasing personal data from the data lake

options.name: Rewrite the affected files
options.pro: The bytes are really gone, and no key service is needed
options.con: One person's rows touch millions of files, so a weekly batch may rewrite most of 600 TB

options.name: Per-user keys and crypto-shredding
options.pro: Erasure is one key delete and takes seconds, whatever the data size
options.con: Needs a key lookup on every read and write, and the key store becomes critical

options.name: Tombstone rows and compact later
options.pro: Cheap to record and works with table formats that support deletes
options.con: The data stays readable until compaction, which may pass the deadline

alternatives.pick: Crypto-shredding for new data, with a tombstone and compaction for the oldest data written before keys existed.

alternatives.title: Who triggers the deletion in each store

options.name: Central orchestrator with tasks
options.pro: One status, one clock and one place for retries and proof
options.con: Needs a connector for each store and a map that stays accurate

options.name: Each service listens for a UserDeleted event
options.pro: Teams own their own cleanup and nothing central to maintain
options.con: No one knows which services missed the event, and proof is scattered

options.name: A nightly job that scans every database
options.pro: Finds data nobody remembered to register
options.con: Heavy, slow, and cannot erase safely without knowing each store

alternatives.pick: A central orchestrator, with events as the way the connectors are told, and a scanner as the safety net.

alternatives.title: Deleted data in backups

options.name: Edit or re-create backups
options.pro: Erasure is complete in every copy immediately
options.con: Very expensive, breaks the integrity of a backup and is risky to do while recovery depends on it

options.name: Let backups expire, with a replay list
options.pro: Backups stay immutable and trusted, and nobody is resurrected
options.con: The data lives in backups for up to 35 days, past the 30-day deadline

options.name: Encrypt each backup with a per-user key
options.pro: A key delete would cover backups too
options.con: Backups are not organised by person, and a restore would need millions of keys

alternatives.pick: Let backups expire and replay the deletions on restore, with the retention stated in the notice.

alternatives.title: Proof of deletion

options.name: A signed ledger of task results
options.pro: Shows which store was erased how and when, with no personal data
options.con: Must be built, kept for years and protected from edits

options.name: Keep the deleted person's id and a log of rows removed
options.pro: Easy to audit and easy to search
options.con: The proof itself holds the personal data it claims to have removed

options.name: Trust the services and keep nothing
options.pro: No new storage and no new risk
options.con: No way to answer a regulator, and no way to see which task failed

alternatives.pick: A signed, append-only ledger of salted hashes, store names, methods and times.

roles.label: Requesters
roles.description: Users, support staff and the legal team who file requests and holds.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The intake API and the connections to third-party processors.

roles.label: Task queue
roles.description: The deletion and export tasks on their way to the stores.

roles.label: Orchestration
roles.description: The orchestrator, the store connectors and the legal hold check.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The data map, the stores, the lake and key store, the backups and the proof ledger.

quiz.question: A company with 200 services handles "delete my data" by running a support script that removes the user's row from the main accounts database and clears one cache key. A regulator audit finds the person's email in a search index, the analytics warehouse and an email vendor, and nobody can say which requests were ever finished. What is the best fix?
options: Add the search index, the warehouse and the email vendor to the script, then re-run it each night until it exits without an error for that user
Schedule a weekly job that scans every database for the person's email address, deletes each row it finds and logs how many it removed
Keep a data map of stores and erase methods, and run an orchestrator that makes one tracked task per store with retries and a deadline
Ask each service team to subscribe to a user-deleted event, clean its own data, and report to the privacy team if something fails
quiz.explanation: The core gap is that nobody knows where the data is or which parts are done. A data map plus a per-store task with a state, retries and a clock answers both. Adding stores to a script, or relying on a scan or on events, still leaves no record of which stores completed or failed.

quiz.question: A data lake holds 600 TB of immutable columnar files, and the platform erases about 270 people a day. Each person's rows are spread across nearly every file. The team compares a weekly batch that rewrites every file with giving each person an encryption key and deleting the key. Assuming the batch must finish within the week, which statement is right?
options: The rewrite needs about 1 GB/s read and write all week, while deleting keys rewrites no files, so key deletion fits
Rewriting is cheaper, because each batch only touches the roughly 1,900 people erased that week and so only a small share of the files
Key deletion needs a separate backup of every key before it is destroyed, which adds up to as much work as a weekly rewrite of the files
The two cost about the same, since the key store for 40 million accounts is hundreds of terabytes and must be rewritten as well
quiz.explanation: 600 TB over 7 days is about 1 GB/s of sustained reads and writes, because the batch touches nearly every file. Deleting a 32-byte key per person is instant and the whole key store is around 1.3 GB for 40 million accounts. Keeping a copy of a destroyed key would defeat the erasure.

quiz.question: A person's deletion request is half done on day 10 when legal places a hold on their data because of a lawsuit. Several hard-delete tasks for that person are already queued to run on day 12. Which design keeps the held data safe?
options: Check for holds when the request is accepted, because a request that passed the check is known to be safe and can run to the end
Cancel the whole request and delete its task records, so that the person has to submit a new request after the hold is released
Check the hold service right before each hard-delete task runs, block the queued ones, and resume them after release
Mark the person's accounts as locked in the main database, since the connectors in other stores will notice the lock when they next read it
quiz.explanation: A hold can arrive at any time, so the check has to sit right before each irreversible task, not only at intake. Blocked tasks keep their state and resume later with the original legal clock in mind. Checking at intake misses a hold placed on day 10, and deleting the task records would lose the proof of what already happened.
